title: Mutated neuron navigator 3 as a candidate gene for a rare neurodevelopmental disorder.

reviewer.method: Read all structured article text in two non-truncated consecutive ranges, including all 27 references and endmatter. Inspected all panels of Figures 1–3, the graphical abstract, and the entire Table 1 as pixels after fresh PDF layout extraction. Adjudicated the sole selected packet and all seventeen phenotype assertions individually.

audit.exposure_note: Parent has seen compact-cohort aggregate results, not the NAV3 per-case ranking. This is a post-inference, non-blinded audit.

patient_identity.statement: Single index IV-4 is a thirteen-year-old Saudi female born to first-cousin parents, matching packet identity and age/sex.

genotype.statement: The source reports homozygous NAV3 c.2604_2605delAG/p.Val870SerfsTer12, matching the packet’s coding/protein description and zygosity.
limitations: The paper names NM_014903.6/NP_055718.4, whereas the packet names NM_001024383.2/NP_001019554.1. Transcript equivalence and the hg38 normalized genomic representation have not been independently established here; original WES was aligned to GRCh37.

segregation.statement: Source claims Sanger confirmation and Figure 1a depicts both parents and brother IV-5 as heterozygous, proband IV-4 homozygous and healthy sister IV-7 wild type.
limitations: No Sanger traces or raw genotypes are shown. Another shaded individual IV-2 is ungenotyped and not characterized; the phrase perfectly segregated cannot establish that person’s diagnosis or genotype.

phase.statement: Reported homozygosity with heterozygous parents is consistent with transmission of one mutant allele from each parent.
limitations: No direct haplotype, copy-number or read-level confirmation is supplied; this is reported homozygosity rather than independent phasing.

causal_confidence.statement: Results 3.3 explicitly classifies the variant as VUS, Class 3, and the paper presents NAV3 as a candidate requiring additional patients/functional studies. The packet instead labels it PATHOGENIC, CAUSATIVE and SOLVED.
limitations: This flags overstatement relative to this publication, not a new ACMG classification or a conclusion that NAV3 is noncausal.

PBMC transcript reduction and predicted structure changes do not establish the neural disease mechanism. The RT-qPCR figure describes three independent experiments but not three independent affected people.

phenotype_completeness.statement: All seventeen features reviewed. Tics, poor sleep and anxiety are positive in the packet but explicitly negative in Table 1. Remaining features have narrative/table support, with source-internal normal/abnormal inconsistencies retained.

limitations: Complete article reading is not experimental replication or independent diagnostic truth; audit occurred after inference with prior aggregate-result exposure.

The source model uses a 963-residue partial NAV3 sequence and discusses a frameshift partly as a Val-to-Ser substitution. Predicted stability/secondary structure cannot be treated as empirical protein loss or rescue.

The table summarizes MRI, skeletal survey, eye and musculoskeletal examination as normal despite narrative anomalies. Specific narrative observations are retained rather than letting a generic normal label erase them.
Primers and additional raw data are offered only on request. None was obtained or claimed read; there is no publicly listed supplementary file.

Several background citations appear topically mismatched on their printed titles (for example Klein 2005 liver injury for neural guidance, Zong 2015 Alzheimer mouse work for ASD/ADHD). These references were read as bibliography, not independently adjudicated as new source papers.
No source here measures N1002K/BubR1 function, drug rescue or comparative therapeutic benefit.
